## Recruiting Your Own Bodyguards {background-color="#1B4332"}

*Recruter ses propres gardes du corps*

::: {.notes}
Transition, ~5 sec.
:::

## Two strategies, same logic as last week

Recall Week 3's constitutive vs. induced axis — plants recruit
natural enemies the same two ways:

| | **Reward** (standing investment) | **Signal** (conditional, on attack) |
|---|---|---|
| What the plant gives | Food and/or shelter, continuously | A volatile "help" signal, only when attacked |
| Who's paid, and by what | The enemy, directly, by the plant | Nobody directly — the enemy is paid by *eating the herbivore* |
| Timing | Always on | Induced |

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min. This is the single most important conceptual link of the
day - indirect resistance has its own constitutive/induced split,
exactly parallel to Week 3's direct-resistance framework.
:::

## Reward-based recruitment: examples

- **Extrafloral nectar** — sugar-rich nectar produced *outside* the
  flower (not for pollinators), specifically to feed ants or
  parasitoid wasps that then patrol and defend the plant
- **Food bodies** — e.g., Beltian bodies on acacia, nutrient-rich
  structures grown purely to feed resident ant colonies
- **Domatia** — small shelters on leaves that house predatory mites,
  which then control herbivorous mites nearby

**The plant pays rent, continuously, for a standing bodyguard
service — whether or not it's currently under attack.**

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min. Ant-acacia mutualism is a classic, vivid example if you
want to add a photo - ants get housing (domatia in thorns) AND food
(Beltian bodies) and in return attack anything that touches the
plant, including trimming back competing vegetation.
:::

## Signal-based recruitment: HIPVs

- **Herbivore-induced plant volatiles (HIPVs)** — recall Week 1's
  Fraenkel/Turlings maize story, and Week 3's "Chemical resistance:
  induced examples" slide
- Only released when the plant is actually being eaten — a specific
  volatile blend that distinguishes *herbivore damage* from ordinary
  mechanical wounding
- The receiving parasitoid or predator isn't paid by the plant at
  all — it's hunting for its own food (the herbivore), and the plant
  just made that herbivore much easier to find

**Cheap when unattacked, but the enemy has to actually be listening
nearby — no guaranteed bodyguard, just an SOS broadcast.**

::: {.notes}
~2 min. This is where the course's own classification (Week 2's
synomone) gets its mechanism: HIPVs are synomones precisely because
both the plant (fewer herbivores) and the recruited enemy (easier
meal) benefit.
:::
